introduction: This separate comparison returns to Athens in 403 BCE, after fighting at Munychia. It occurs before Cyrus’s expedition of 401 BCE. Cleocritus addresses the opposing citizens after the dead have been recovered. Xenophon reports the scene but is not inserted as an attendee.

Course adaptation of Xenophon, Hellenica 2.4.19–22. Shared worship, education, military service, family ties, grief, and the appeal against obedience to the Thirty follow the source. The Greek wording, statements of future intention, and purpose participles are newly supplied teaching adaptations. They are not preserved quotations from Cleocritus.

The main scene uses present retelling and labeled adapted future language. The officials lead their men away from the speech; no immediate civic unity is invented. The final reflection compares this appeal’s purpose with Cyrus’s demands, without putting Cleocritus in the expedition.

reading.translation:
Now the account concerns Athens, not Cyrus’s journey. After the battle at Munychia the citizens carry the dead. Cleocritus, the herald of the initiates, approaches the other citizens.

Cleocritus comes to announce his judgment. He has a fine voice, and the citizens are silent. “Fellow citizens,” he says, “why do you drive us from the city? Why do you want to kill us?”

“We share rites, sacrifices, and festivals. At the festivals we dance together, and we share the same education. In war too we are comrades; we guard our common freedom.”

“Kinship binds many of us, and friendship is strong. Some of the dead are ours, others yours. We weep also for your dead. We regard you as citizens, not enemies.”

“It is necessary to save our homeland; we must not obey the Thirty. For the Thirty seek their private advantage. We shall seek our common safety and judge what is just.”

Cleocritus delivers his speech, but the officials lead their own men away. Not everyone immediately becomes a friend. Some listen, others depart; the city is still in danger.

Again we consider leaders. For what purpose do the citizens go? For what purpose will the soldiers fight? “I shall go to ask about safety” is a statement of the person inquiring, not a statement of Cleocritus. Not every leader has the same purpose.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Common safety and private advantage

blocks.title: Common safety and private advantage
body: κοινός, shared, and ἴδιος, private or one’s own, organize the appeal. κοινὴ σωτηρία concerns safety held in common; ἰδία ὠφέλεια is an advantage sought for particular people. Cleocritus attributes private profit to the Thirty; that is part of his appeal.

πολίτης, citizen, and πατρίς, homeland, connect civic identity with obligations. συγγένεια is kinship, while παιδεία and ἑορτή name education and festival life. These are distinct shared ties, not interchangeable proofs that political conflict has ended.

δεῖ and χρή introduce what must happen. They require an infinitive in the examples, rather than a personal ending identifying “I” or “you.” εἶμι identifies a movement in future context; the purpose participle explains why someone goes.

sections.title: 1. Liquid and Nasal Futures
body: Many verbs whose stems end in λ, μ, ν, or ρ form an asigmatic contracted future. The future stem combines with endings in -εω and contracts: μένω → μενῶ, “I shall remain”; ἀγγέλλω → ἀγγελῶ, “I shall announce.” The latter future uses a single λ.

The active endings appear as -ῶ, -εῖς, -εῖ, -οῦμεν, -εῖτε, -οῦσι(ν). The circumflex marks contraction where the accent rules allow it. From κρίνω obtain κρινῶ, κρινεῖς, κρινεῖ; from νέμω obtain νεμῶ. Learn stem differences as well as the ending.

Compare present μένω with future μενῶ: spelling and accent distinguish them. Unlike λύσω there is no surface sigma. Middle contracted futures such as ἀμυνοῦμαι also exist; today’s assessed paradigm centers on the active forms below, while middle examples are supported recognition.

examples.english: We shall judge what is just.

sections.title: 2. εἶμι and εἰμί
body: εἶμι means “I go” and in ordinary Attic usage often carries future meaning, “I shall go.” Its indicative forms are εἶμι, εἶ, εἶσι(ν); ἴμεν, ἴτε, ἴασι(ν). Its infinitive is ἰέναι, “to go.” This is a supplied irregular paradigm, not a regular sigmatic future.

εἰμί means “I am.” Compare the first-person spellings: εἶμι has a circumflex and means going; εἰμί has an acute and means being. Third-person εἶσι(ν), goes or will go, differs clearly from ἐστί(ν), is. Some forms, such as second-person εἶ, coincide in spelling, so context must decide.

In the labeled supplementary statement εἶμι ἐρωτήσων, the movement verb has future sense and the future participle supplies purpose. A place or purpose commonly helps identify going, while a predicate noun or adjective often points to being. Never decide from the English word “will” alone.

sections.title: 3. Future Participles Expressing Purpose
body: A future active participle can express the purpose of coming or going: ἔρχεται ἐρωτήσων, “he comes to ask.” The asking is intended after or as the goal of the approach, not an ongoing action simultaneous with it. Compare present ἐρωτῶν, “asking.”

Sigmatic futures form active participles in -σων, -σουσα, -σον: λύσων, λύσουσα, λῦσον; ἐρωτήσων, ἐρωτήσουσα, ἐρωτῆσον. Masculine/neuter declension follows the -οντ- pattern, such as λύσοντος and λύσοντα. Feminine uses first-declension endings, such as λυσούσης.

Liquid/nasal futures contract in the participle too: ἀγγελῶν, ἀγγελοῦσα, ἀγγελοῦν. Agreement still identifies the person: ὁ Κλεόκριτος ἔρχεται ἀγγελῶν; a woman would have ἀγγελοῦσα. These future-purpose statements are instructional additions around the reported appeal, not recovered words of the speaker.

checks.answer: λύσουσα. σ plus -ουσα forms future feminine nominative.

sections.title: 4. δεῖ and χρή with an Infinitive
body: δεῖ means “it is necessary” and χρή means “one must” or “it is fitting.” They are impersonal: the Greek form does not have a personal subject meaning “I” or “you.” An infinitive names the required action: δεῖ σῴζειν, “it is necessary to save.”

An accusative can specify the person required to act: δεῖ τοὺς πολίτας ἀκούειν, “the citizens must listen.” τοὺς πολίτας is the understood subject of the infinitive, not a nominative subject of δεῖ. An infinitive can still have its own object: δεῖ τοὺς πολίτας τὴν πατρίδα σῴζειν.

The infinitive’s ordinary negative is μή: χρὴ μὴ πείθεσθαι, “one must not obey.” Obedience takes a dative recipient in the reading, τοῖς τριάκοντα. Distinguish grammar from endorsement: translating an obligation accurately does not prove that the speaker’s claimed obligation is just.

sections.title: 5. Direct Questions and Question Words
body: A direct question can ask for a fact or explanation: τίς; “who?”, τί; “what?” or “why?” in context, ποῦ; “where?”, πότε; “when?”, and διὰ τί; “why?” The Greek question mark is the semicolon. A question can use present or future forms.

Interrogative τίς, τί is accented, unlike indefinite τις, τι, “someone, something.” It declines: τίνος, “of whom?”; τίνι, “to whom?”; τίνα, “whom?”; plural τίνες, “who?” The interrogative’s case marks its role inside the question.

ἆρα can introduce a yes-or-no question. τίνος ἕνεκα asks “for what purpose?” with genitive τίνος and the postposition ἕνεκα. In the appeal τί ἡμᾶς ἐλαύνετε; means “why do you drive us out?”; διὰ τί makes the request for a reason explicit. Ask whose purpose a leader’s proposal serves.

examples.english: Why do you want to kill us?
For what purpose do the citizens go?

sections.title: A dated scene in a divided city
body: This comparison takes place in 403 BCE, after the fighting at Munychia, before the expedition of 401. Athens is divided between the Thirty’s regime and its opponents. Hellenica 2.4.19 describes recovery of the dead and conversation between men from the opposing sides before Cleocritus speaks.

The fighting at Munychia and the subsequent appeal belong to 403 BCE, during the struggle to end the Thirty’s rule. The Greek reading retells the scene in the present for learners and supplies no claim that Xenophon attended. Military victory has created an opportunity to speak, not a city already reconciled.

sections.title: The herald’s appeal to a shared life
body: Cleocritus is identified as the herald of the initiates and as having a fine voice. He addresses the others as citizens, asking why they drive out and seek to kill people with whom they have shared rites, sacrifices, festivals, dancing, education, and military dangers. The speech relies on relationships that cross the current political divide.

He adds family and marriage connections, companionship, common safety and freedom, and grief even for the other side’s dead. The adaptation selects these ties and turns the remembered shared experience into present descriptions. They are reasons offered to change allegiance and action; they are not evidence that every individual on each side responds alike.

sections.title: An appeal interrupted, and an obligation examined
body: Cleocritus urges his hearers to stop wronging the homeland and to reject the Thirty. His accusation that the rulers kill for private gain belongs to the speech Xenophon reports. At 2.4.22 the opposing officials, after hearing this, lead their men away. The passage does not report immediate reconciliation produced by the appeal.

The civic comparison asks what leadership is for. Cyrus offers benefits tied to his royal war; Cleocritus appeals to shared ties and safety among fellow citizens. The future intentions and purpose participles in the Greek are explicitly course additions. The learner can compare competing obligations while keeping distinct the speech, the officials’ response, and the still unresolved conflict.
